newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Death and dominoes as rebels enter Kinshasa.
newsitem.headline: Death and dominoes as rebels enter Kinshasa.

text.p: A stone's throw from Kinshasa's Chinese-built soccer stadium, the bodies of two soldiers from Mobutu Sese Seko's ragged army lay next to a shot-up BMW car.
Nearby, a small group of Laurent Kabila's rebels in their trademark rubber wellington boots rested in the shade.
Seven months after taking up arms over Zairean nationality for ethnic Tutsis, the rebels finally reached the capital of the country Kabila has rebaptised the Democratic Republic of Congo.
After a march across Africa's third largest country, they entered the capital on Saturday virtually unopposed.

Sporadic gunfire rang out around the usually bustling city of five million people but soldiers from the veteran president's army seemed more interested in ditching their uniforms and melting into the crowd, or simply fleeing.
Elsewhere, cheering residents, many wearing white bandannas denoting support for the rebels, turned out with palm fronds, food and drink to hail the end of three decades of Mobutu rule.
"We have been waiting for this for a long time," said one bystander in the eastern residential district of Lemba.
"This is a new page in the history of Zaire," said another.
Witnesses if different parts of the city reported looting at homes of Mobutu loyalists. Some blamed members of Mobutu's army, others blamed angry local residents.
But at Lemba's Salongo Nord Camp, senior officers and soldiers handed over weapons to the arriving rebels.
Small groups of rebels, most aged under 25, walked into Kinshasa's suburbs meeting little or no resistance.
Virtually unopposed, they moved on. One group entered the 19-storey tower housing state broadcaster Voice of Zaire, as well as the information ministry, one worker there said.
Lack of a technician frustrated attempts to broadcast an announcement and the radio played music -- a mix of African rhythms, soft rock in French, English or Italian and Elton John.
Dropping the Voice of Zaire label and calling itself Kinshasa Radio, state radio told listeners later that "the army of liberation is well and truly in Kinshasa".
An unidentified announcer said at 5 p.m. (1600 GMT) that the rebels were not yet in full control.

"It's a big city and if there are districts which haven't yet seen units of the AFDL (alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire) passing, don't worry, it's a sure thing in the next few moments," he added.
The radio promised a message to the people from Kabila.
Kinshasa awoke on Saturday from a fourth night of curfew anxiously awaiting the rebels. Many residents feared a looting rampage by Mobutu's notoriously ill-disciplined troops.
The streets of central Kinshasa were virtually empty and very quiet by late afternoon, with only a few shots heard.
No soldiers were visible on the wide Boulevard of June 30, a central thoroughfare where the few rare vehicles whizzed through red stop lights without halting.
In Lemba, a mob beat up a soldier, leaving him in a pool of blood.

A source at the presidency in Kinshasa and other sources in the city said that members of Mobutu's armed forces were fleeing west on the road out of the city to lower Zaire. Others fled across the river to neighbouring Congo.
The radio thanked callers for alerting the new authorities to incidents of looting and told them if help was on its way.
In places, life started to resume a semblance of normality. On one street corner, a couple of men set up a table and played dominoes in the sweltering heat.
